items.prompt: Your class has discussed whether governments should regulate artificial intelligence. Write an essay discussing two of the following areas and explaining which is more urgent to regulate.
items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận về việc chính phủ có nên quản lý trí tuệ nhân tạo. Hãy viết bài luận bàn về hai trong các lĩnh vực sau và giải thích lĩnh vực nào cần quản lý cấp bách hơn.
items.sampleAnswer:
Few technologies have advanced as rapidly as artificial intelligence, and legislation has struggled to keep pace. While AI raises concerns across many areas, I would argue that its impact on privacy and on the spread of misinformation demands particularly urgent attention.

As far as privacy is concerned, AI systems depend on vast quantities of personal data, much of which is collected without users' meaningful consent. Facial recognition, for instance, allows individuals to be identified and tracked in public spaces, raising profound questions about surveillance. Once such systems become embedded in everyday life, reversing them is extraordinarily difficult, which strengthens the case for setting clear limits now.

Misinformation, however, poses an even more immediate threat. AI can now generate convincing text, images and even video at negligible cost, making it possible to flood the internet with fabricated content. During elections or public health emergencies, the consequences could be severe: if citizens can no longer distinguish genuine information from fabrication, trust in institutions is likely to erode. Unlike privacy violations, which typically harm individuals, misinformation can undermine democratic processes themselves.

Admittedly, regulating either area presents challenges, not least because technology companies operate across borders and overly restrictive rules might stifle innovation. Nevertheless, measures such as requiring AI-generated content to be clearly labelled would be relatively straightforward to introduce.

On balance, while both areas require attention, misinformation should be the priority. Its potential to destabilise entire societies, combined with the speed at which it spreads, means that delay could prove extremely costly.

items.prompt: Your class has been discussing ways to make cities more liveable. Write an essay discussing two of the following methods and explaining which would be more effective.
items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận các cách làm thành phố đáng sống hơn. Hãy viết bài luận về hai trong các biện pháp sau và giải thích biện pháp nào hiệu quả hơn.
items.sampleAnswer:
As urban populations continue to swell, the question of how to make cities pleasant places to live has become increasingly pressing. Of the various approaches proposed, investment in public transport and the creation of green spaces are frequently cited, yet their effectiveness differs in important ways.

Green spaces undoubtedly enhance urban life. Parks provide room for exercise and relaxation, help to cool cities during heatwaves and have been linked to improved mental health. In densely populated districts where residents have no gardens, a well-maintained park can be a lifeline. However, the benefits of a single park are largely confined to those who live nearby, and in many cities suitable land is scarce and extremely expensive.

Public transport, by contrast, has the potential to transform an entire city. A reliable, affordable network reduces traffic congestion and air pollution, while widening access to jobs, education and services for those who cannot afford a car. Moreover, by reducing the space devoted to roads and parking, effective public transport can actually free up land that could later be converted into green areas.

It might be objected that transport infrastructure is costly and takes years to build. This is true, yet the long-term economic and social returns tend to far outweigh the initial outlay.

In conclusion, while green spaces make an invaluable contribution to wellbeing, investment in public transport would be the more effective measure. Not only does it address a wider range of problems, but it also creates the conditions in which other improvements become possible.

items.prompt: Your class has discussed how to reduce inequality in education. Write an essay discussing two of the following approaches and explaining which would have the greater impact.
items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận cách giảm bất bình đẳng trong giáo dục. Hãy viết bài luận về hai trong các cách tiếp cận sau và giải thích cách nào có tác động lớn hơn.
points: better pay for teachers in disadvantaged areas
items.sampleAnswer:
Educational inequality is one of the most persistent obstacles to social mobility. Among the many proposals for addressing it, free early-years education and free university tuition attract considerable attention, though I would contend that the former is likely to achieve far more.

The argument for free university tuition is superficially compelling. High fees may deter talented students from low-income families, and removing them would seem to open doors. However, by the time students reach eighteen, the gap between rich and poor is already deeply entrenched. Many disadvantaged young people never achieve the grades required for university, so free tuition would disproportionately benefit middle-class families whose children would have attended anyway.

Early-years education, on the other hand, intervenes at the point where it can make the greatest difference. Research consistently shows that differences in vocabulary and cognitive development between children from different backgrounds emerge well before they start school. High-quality nursery provision can narrow these gaps when children's brains are most adaptable, giving them a far stronger foundation for everything that follows. It also enables parents, particularly mothers, to return to work, thereby raising family incomes.

That is not to say that higher education should be neglected; targeted grants for low-income students remain essential. Yet resources are finite, and they should be directed where their impact is greatest.

Ultimately, inequality is easier to prevent than to reverse. For that reason, investing in the earliest years of a child's life would have a considerably greater and longer-lasting impact than making university free for all.

items.prompt: Your class has been discussing actions to reduce climate change. Write an essay discussing two of the following and explaining which should be prioritised.
items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận các hành động giảm biến đổi khí hậu. Hãy viết bài luận về hai trong các hành động sau và giải thích hành động nào nên ưu tiên.
items.sampleAnswer:
There is now broad agreement that urgent action is needed to limit climate change; what remains contested is which measures should take precedence. Two frequently discussed options are taxing carbon emissions and encouraging individuals to change their behaviour.

Campaigns urging people to fly less, eat less meat or recycle more have raised awareness considerably. Individual choices undoubtedly matter, and they can shift social norms over time. Nevertheless, relying primarily on voluntary behaviour change has clear limitations. Many people lack the time, money or information to make greener choices, and even highly motivated individuals cannot avoid the emissions built into the energy systems and products around them.

A carbon tax, by contrast, addresses the problem at its source. By making polluting activities more expensive, it creates a powerful incentive for businesses to cut emissions and invest in cleaner alternatives, while leaving them free to decide how best to do so. Crucially, it also influences consumers indirectly, since the price of high-carbon goods rises relative to greener ones. Critics rightly point out that such taxes can hit low-income households hardest. However, this can be offset by returning the revenue to citizens as a dividend, which in some schemes leaves poorer families better off.

In light of these considerations, carbon taxation should be the priority. Individual action is valuable, but it is most effective when supported by a system that makes sustainable choices the easiest and cheapest ones. Without such a framework, we are placing an unreasonable burden on individuals to solve a structural problem.

items.prompt: Your class has discussed the changing nature of work. Write an essay discussing two of the following developments and explaining which will have the greater effect on society.
items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận về bản chất thay đổi của công việc. Hãy viết bài luận về hai trong các xu hướng sau và giải thích xu hướng nào ảnh hưởng lớn hơn đến xã hội.
items.sampleAnswer:
The world of work is undergoing profound transformation, driven by technological and social change. Two developments in particular, remote working and automation, are reshaping how and where people earn their living, though their long-term consequences are likely to differ in scale.

Remote working, accelerated dramatically by the pandemic, has altered daily life for millions of office workers. Freed from commuting, many enjoy greater flexibility and a better balance between work and family. Its effects extend beyond individuals: city-centre businesses that depended on commuters have suffered, while smaller towns have experienced an influx of new residents. Yet remote working remains largely confined to professional, office-based roles, so its impact is uneven across the workforce.

Automation, by contrast, has the potential to affect almost every sector. Machines and software are increasingly capable of performing not only routine manual tasks but also cognitive work once considered uniquely human, from analysing legal documents to diagnosing illnesses. While new jobs will undoubtedly emerge, the transition could displace large numbers of workers whose skills are no longer in demand, potentially widening inequality between those who can adapt and those who cannot.

It could be argued that automation has been predicted to cause mass unemployment for decades without doing so. However, the breadth of tasks that can now be automated is unprecedented.

Overall, while remote working has visibly changed many people's routines, automation is likely to have the greater effect on society. Its reach is broader, and the questions it raises about employment, income and education will shape policy for generations.

items.prompt: Your class has discussed ways of improving public health. Write an essay discussing two of the following approaches and explaining which would be more effective.
items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận cách cải thiện sức khỏe cộng đồng. Hãy viết bài luận về hai trong các cách sau và giải thích cách nào hiệu quả hơn.
items.sampleAnswer:
Rising rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease place enormous strain on healthcare systems, prompting governments to search for effective preventive measures. Health education in schools and taxes on unhealthy products represent two quite different philosophies: one seeks to inform choices, the other to reshape them.

Health education has obvious appeal. Teaching children about nutrition, exercise and mental wellbeing equips them with knowledge they can carry throughout their lives, and it respects their autonomy. However, knowledge alone rarely changes behaviour. Most adults are well aware that sugary drinks and processed food are harmful, yet consumption remains high, largely because such products are cheap, convenient and heavily marketed.

Taxes on unhealthy products, on the other hand, have produced measurable results. Where levies on sugary drinks have been introduced, consumption has generally fallen, and in several cases manufacturers have reformulated their products to reduce sugar content in order to avoid the tax. In this way, the policy improves the health of people who never consciously change their habits. Opponents argue that such taxes are paternalistic and penalise poorer households. These concerns are legitimate, but they can be mitigated if the revenue is invested in subsidising healthy food or funding community health programmes.

In conclusion, education is a valuable long-term investment, but on its own it is unlikely to counteract the powerful commercial forces shaping our diets. Taxes on unhealthy products would therefore be the more effective approach, particularly if combined with educational initiatives that help people make the most of healthier options.

items.prompt: Your class has discussed how governments should support the arts. Write an essay discussing two of the following and explaining which is the better use of public money.
items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận cách chính phủ hỗ trợ nghệ thuật. Hãy viết bài luận về hai trong các hình thức sau và giải thích hình thức nào sử dụng ngân sách công tốt hơn.
items.sampleAnswer:
Public funding for the arts is often among the first casualties when budgets are tight, which makes it all the more important that the money available is spent wisely. Two common approaches are funding prestigious national institutions and supporting local community arts projects.

National museums and theatres play a significant role in a country's cultural life. They preserve heritage, maintain high artistic standards and attract tourists, generating revenue that benefits the wider economy. Without public support, many could not survive, since ticket sales rarely cover the full cost of world-class productions or the conservation of priceless collections.

Nevertheless, such institutions are typically concentrated in capital cities, and their audiences tend to be disproportionately affluent and well educated. For many people, particularly those in deprived or rural areas, these venues feel remote, both geographically and socially. Community arts projects, by contrast, bring creative activity directly into people's lives. Local theatre groups, mural projects and music workshops encourage active participation rather than passive consumption, and they have been shown to reduce isolation, build confidence and strengthen community ties.

This is not to suggest that national institutions should be abandoned. However, they are often better placed than small projects to raise money from private sponsors and international visitors.

On balance, community arts projects represent the better use of public money. They reach people who would otherwise have little access to the arts, and they deliver social benefits that extend far beyond culture itself. Public funding should, above all, ensure that the arts belong to everyone.

items.prompt: Your class has discussed the influence of the media on young people. Write an essay discussing two of the following and explaining which has the greater influence.
items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận về ảnh hưởng của truyền thông tới giới trẻ. Hãy viết bài luận về hai trong các yếu tố sau và giải thích yếu tố nào có ảnh hưởng lớn hơn.
items.sampleAnswer:
Young people today are exposed to a constant stream of media messages, and concerns about how these shape their values and behaviour are widespread. Among the most frequently discussed influences are social media influencers and traditional advertising.

Advertising has long been criticised for promoting unrealistic standards and encouraging consumerism. Its techniques are sophisticated, and young people, who are still forming their identities, may be particularly susceptible. However, advertising is now widely recognised for what it is. Most teenagers understand that a television commercial is designed to sell them something, and this awareness acts as a partial defence against its persuasive power.

Influencers, on the other hand, operate in a far more subtle manner. Because they present themselves as ordinary individuals sharing their lives, their followers often perceive them as friends rather than salespeople. Recommendations feel personal and authentic, even when they are paid for. Furthermore, influencers shape not only purchasing decisions but also attitudes towards appearance, success and lifestyle. The intimacy of the relationship, combined with the sheer amount of time young people spend on social media, makes this influence difficult to resist or even recognise.

As life expectancy rises and birth rates fall, many countries face the challenge of supporting a growing number of older citizens with a shrinking working-age population. Raising the retirement age and investing in elderly care are two responses that are frequently debated.

Raising the retirement age is often presented as an unavoidable financial necessity. People are living considerably longer than when pension systems were designed, and asking them to work a few more years would reduce pressure on public finances. Many older people are healthy and willing to continue working, and doing so can provide purpose and social contact. However, this approach is far from fair to everyone. Those in physically demanding jobs, who are often on lower incomes and have shorter life expectancies, may simply be unable to continue, and would effectively be penalised.

Investment in elderly care addresses a different but equally pressing need. As the number of people over eighty increases, so does demand for medical treatment, home support and residential care. In many countries, care systems are already overstretched, and much of the burden falls on unpaid family members, most often women, who may have to reduce their own working hours as a result. Properly funded care would therefore not only improve older people's quality of life but also enable more carers to remain in employment.

While both measures have a role, investing in elderly care is the more important priority. Financial sustainability matters, but a society should ultimately be judged by how well it looks after those who are most vulnerable.

items.promptVi: Lớp bạn thảo luận về cách chi ngân sách cho khoa học. Hãy viết bài luận về hai trong các lĩnh vực sau và giải thích lĩnh vực nào nên được cấp nhiều kinh phí hơn.
items.sampleAnswer:
Public funding for scientific research is limited, and decisions about how to allocate it inevitably involve difficult trade-offs. Space exploration and renewable energy research are both ambitious fields with passionate advocates, yet their claims on public money are not equally strong at present.

Space exploration captures the imagination like few other endeavours. It expands our understanding of the universe and has produced numerous technological spin-offs, from satellite navigation to advances in materials science. Furthermore, Earth-observation satellites have become indispensable for monitoring weather, agriculture and climate change. Nevertheless, many of the most expensive projects, such as crewed missions to other planets, offer few immediate practical benefits, and an increasing share of space activity is now funded by private companies.

Renewable energy research, by contrast, addresses one of the most urgent challenges facing humanity. While solar and wind power have become dramatically cheaper, significant obstacles remain, particularly in storing energy efficiently and decarbonising industries such as steel and cement. Breakthroughs in these areas could accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels, reducing the severe economic and human costs of climate change. Given the timescale involved, delays in research could have consequences that are both enormous and irreversible.

This is not to dismiss the value of space science, which enriches human knowledge in ways that are difficult to quantify. However, when resources are scarce, urgency must be a key consideration.

In conclusion, renewable energy research should receive greater funding. Its potential to protect the planet we already inhabit makes it a more pressing priority than exploring those beyond it.

items.promptVi: Công ty bạn vừa thử nghiệm giờ làm linh hoạt trong sáu tháng. Quản lý yêu cầu bạn viết báo cáo đánh giá và đưa ra đề xuất.
items.sampleAnswer:
Evaluation of the Flexible Working Trial

Introduction
This report assesses the six-month trial of flexible working hours, which allowed staff to start work at any time between 7 a.m. and 10.30 a.m. It draws on productivity data, an anonymous staff survey completed by 112 employees and interviews with department heads.

Productivity
Overall, productivity remained stable or improved slightly in most departments. Notably, the customer service team was able to extend its hours of availability without additional staff, as early and late starters covered a longer working day. The only exception was the design team, where managers reported that coordinating meetings had become considerably more difficult.

Staff reactions
Responses were overwhelmingly positive. Eighty-four per cent of respondents said the scheme had reduced stress, with many citing shorter commutes outside peak hours and greater ease in managing childcare. Several employees, however, expressed concern that colleagues were sometimes unavailable when urgent decisions were required.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, it is recommended that flexible hours be adopted permanently, subject to the following adjustments. Firstly, a set of core hours, perhaps from 10.30 a.m. to 3 p.m., should be introduced, during which all staff are expected to be available. Secondly, teams should agree on a shared calendar to make availability transparent. Finally, the arrangement should be reviewed annually to ensure it continues to meet both business needs and employees' expectations.

Conclusion
The trial has clearly demonstrated that flexibility can benefit staff wellbeing without compromising performance, provided that collaboration is carefully safeguarded.

Report on Student Wellbeing

Purpose
The aim of this report is to identify the principal sources of stress among students and to propose practical measures the college could take to address them. The findings are based on a survey of 250 students and discussions with the student council.

Academic pressure
By far the most frequently cited source of stress was the concentration of deadlines at the end of each term. Many students reported having four or five major assignments due within the same fortnight, leaving little opportunity to produce work of a high standard. Some also felt that feedback arrived too late to be useful for subsequent tasks.

Financial worries
A significant proportion of students, particularly those living away from home, described anxiety about rising rent and living costs. Nearly a third work more than fifteen hours a week in part-time jobs, which inevitably reduces the time available for study and rest.

Support services
Although the college offers a counselling service, awareness of it is surprisingly low. Of those who had used it, many praised the quality of support but complained of waiting times of up to four weeks.

Recommendations
It is recommended that departments coordinate their assessment schedules to spread deadlines more evenly. The college should also consider expanding its hardship fund and offering more paid work on campus, which would allow students to earn money without long commutes. Finally, the counselling service should be better publicised and, if funding permits, additional staff should be recruited to reduce waiting times. Implementing these measures would demonstrate a genuine commitment to students' wellbeing.

The Impact of Tourism on Riverside

Introduction
This report examines the effects of the substantial growth in tourism experienced by Riverside over the past five years and recommends measures to ensure that its benefits are sustained while its drawbacks are minimised.

Economic benefits
Tourism has undoubtedly revitalised the local economy. Visitor numbers have doubled, and the sector now supports an estimated 1,200 jobs, from hotel and restaurant staff to tour guides and craftspeople. Several shops in the old town that were on the verge of closing have reopened, and income from tourist taxes has funded the restoration of the historic bridge.

Problems
However, this growth has not been without cost. During the summer months, the old town becomes severely congested, particularly when coach parties arrive simultaneously. Residents have also raised concerns about the conversion of homes into short-term holiday rentals, which has pushed up rents and forced some families to move away. Litter and noise in the evenings have been the subject of frequent complaints.

Recommendations
In order to address these issues, the following steps are recommended. Coach arrivals should be staggered through a booking system, and a park-and-ride scheme introduced on the edge of town. The council should consider limiting the number of properties that can be used as holiday rentals in residential streets. Finally, a portion of tourist tax revenue should be allocated to additional cleaning services and to marketing the town outside the peak season.

Conclusion
Tourism remains vital to Riverside's prosperity. With careful management, it can continue to benefit the town without undermining residents' quality of life.

Evaluation of the Summer Community Festival

Introduction
The purpose of this report is to evaluate the community festival held in Central Park on 14 July, which aimed to raise funds for the local food bank and bring residents together. It is based on feedback from volunteers, stallholders and an online questionnaire completed by 180 attendees.

Successful aspects
The festival exceeded expectations in several respects. Attendance reached approximately 3,000, almost double the previous year, and over £8,000 was raised for the food bank. The programme of live music by local performers was especially popular, as were the children's activities, which many parents described as the highlight of the day. The decision to feature food stalls run by different cultural groups was widely praised for reflecting the diversity of the area.

Problems
The festival's popularity, however, created difficulties. Queues for food stalls often exceeded forty minutes, and several ran out of supplies by mid-afternoon. There were insufficient toilets and rubbish bins, leading to complaints about cleanliness. In addition, the lack of seating made the event uncomfortable for older visitors and people with disabilities.

Should the festival continue to grow, it will be essential to plan for larger numbers. More stalls should be recruited and advised to prepare greater quantities of food. The number of toilets and bins should be at least doubled, and a shaded seating area provided. It would also be worth introducing a volunteer team responsible solely for keeping the site clean.

Overall, the festival was a resounding success. Addressing these practical issues would ensure that future events are equally enjoyable for everyone.

Encouraging Cycling in Northfield

Introduction
This report outlines the main obstacles currently discouraging residents from cycling and recommends measures to make it a safer and more attractive option. The findings draw on a public consultation in which 430 residents participated, as well as data on road accidents over the past three years.

Safety concerns
Safety emerged as the overriding concern. Over seventy per cent of respondents said they would cycle more if they felt safer on the roads. Existing cycle lanes are frequently painted directly onto busy roads with no physical separation from traffic, and many end abruptly at junctions, which are precisely where most accidents occur. Parents in particular expressed reluctance to let their children cycle to school.

Facilities
Respondents also highlighted a shortage of secure bicycle parking, particularly at the railway station and in the town centre, where bike theft is common. Several employers do not provide showers or changing facilities, which discourages people from cycling to work.

Recommendations
It is recommended that the council prioritise the creation of a connected network of protected cycle lanes linking residential areas with schools, the station and the town centre. Junctions with the highest accident rates should be redesigned as a matter of urgency. Secure, covered bike parking should be installed at key locations, and the council could offer grants to local businesses to provide changing facilities. A cycle training programme for children and adults would further build confidence.

Conclusion

The Use of Technology at Lingua Language School

Introduction
This report examines how technology is currently used in classes and assesses its effectiveness, with a view to recommending improvements. It is based on classroom observations, a survey of 95 students and interviews with eight teachers.

Current use
All classrooms are equipped with interactive whiteboards, and most teachers use them to display materials and audio. Students also have access to an online learning platform for homework and vocabulary practice. However, the extent to which technology is used varies considerably between teachers.

Advantages and problems
Students appreciated the online platform, which allows them to practise at their own pace and receive instant feedback. Teachers noted that video materials make lessons more engaging and expose learners to a variety of accents. Nevertheless, several problems were identified. The Wi-Fi is unreliable in the upstairs classrooms, causing frequent interruptions. Some teachers admitted that they lacked the confidence to use the whiteboards beyond their basic functions, while a number of students felt that certain lessons relied too heavily on screens at the expense of genuine conversation.

Recommendations
First and foremost, the Wi-Fi network should be upgraded. It is also recommended that the school organise regular training sessions so that all teachers can make full use of the available tools. Finally, technology should be viewed as a means of supporting communication rather than replacing it; teachers might agree on guidelines ensuring that each lesson includes substantial speaking practice.

Conclusion
Technology has clear benefits for learners, but its value depends on reliable infrastructure, well-trained teachers and thoughtful integration into lessons.

Proposal for a Community Hub in the Former Post Office

Introduction
The purpose of this proposal is to suggest how the former post office on Market Street, which has stood empty for two years, could be transformed into a community hub serving residents of all ages.

The idea
The building's spacious ground floor would be converted into a café and co-working area, offering affordable desk space for freelancers and remote workers. The first floor would contain flexible rooms available for hire by local groups, for activities such as language classes, support groups and art workshops. A small section could also house a 'repair café', where volunteers help residents fix household items.

Benefits
The hub would address several needs at once. Remote workers, of whom there are now many in the town, often feel isolated working from home and would benefit from a sociable place to work. Older residents would gain a welcoming space to meet, while young people would have somewhere safe to spend time after school. Furthermore, by attracting visitors to the town centre, the hub would support nearby shops, many of which have struggled in recent years.

Funding and management
Initial renovation costs could be covered by a combination of council funding and grants from national regeneration schemes. Once operational, the hub could become largely self-financing through café revenue, desk rental and room hire. I would recommend that it be run as a non-profit social enterprise, managed by a board including residents, local business owners and a council representative.

Converting the empty building into a community hub would breathe new life into the town centre and create a genuine asset for the whole community.

Proposal: Towards a Greener Campus

Introduction
This proposal outlines the main environmental problems on our campus and suggests practical, affordable measures to address them. It reflects the views of the Student Environment Society, which consulted over 200 students.

Current problems
The campus generates a considerable amount of avoidable waste. Disposable cups and food packaging from the canteen account for much of this, and recycling bins are often contaminated because their labelling is unclear. Energy use is also high: lights and computers in many classrooms are left on overnight, and heating is frequently running in empty buildings.

Suggestions
Firstly, the canteen should introduce a discount for students who bring reusable cups and containers, alongside a small charge for disposable ones. Clearly labelled recycling stations should replace the existing bins. Secondly, motion sensors could be installed to switch off lights automatically in unoccupied rooms, and IT staff could schedule computers to shut down at the end of each day. Finally, I propose creating a student 'green team' responsible for raising awareness through events and monitoring progress.

Expected benefits
The financial benefits alone would be substantial. Reduced energy consumption would lower the college's electricity bills, and the cost of sensors would probably be recovered within two years. Equally importantly, these measures would demonstrate the college's commitment to sustainability, which is increasingly important to prospective students when choosing where to study.

Conclusion
These proposals are realistic and inexpensive. By implementing them, the college could significantly reduce its environmental impact while setting an example for students that extends well beyond their time on campus.

Proposal for Improving Interdepartmental Communication

Background
Recent projects have highlighted persistent communication problems between departments. The product launch in March was delayed by three weeks, largely because the marketing and technical teams were working from different timelines, and a staff survey revealed that over half of employees feel poorly informed about what other departments are doing.

Current problems
Departments currently rely heavily on email, which results in important information being lost in overflowing inboxes. Teams use different project management tools, making it difficult to track progress across the company. Moreover, there are few opportunities for staff from different departments to meet informally, so misunderstandings tend to go unresolved.

Proposed improvements
I propose three main changes. Firstly, the company should adopt a single project management platform, giving everyone visibility of deadlines and responsibilities on shared projects. Secondly, a brief monthly meeting should be held at which each department summarises its priorities and upcoming challenges. Thirdly, I suggest introducing a job-shadowing scheme, allowing employees to spend a day in another department. This would foster understanding of colleagues' work and pressures, and help build informal relationships.

Measuring success
The effectiveness of these measures could be assessed by repeating the staff survey after six months and comparing the results. In addition, the number of projects completed on schedule could be monitored, along with feedback from team leaders.

Conclusion
These changes would require only a modest investment of time and money. However, the potential rewards, in terms of efficiency, morale and the quality of our work, are considerable. I would therefore recommend introducing them on a trial basis next quarter.

Proposal: Attracting Young International Visitors to the Lakes Region

Introduction
The aim of this proposal is to explain why the region currently attracts relatively few young international travellers and to suggest practical steps to change this.

The current situation
At present, the region's marketing focuses almost exclusively on older visitors and families, emphasising luxury hotels and guided coach tours. Young travellers, who typically travel on tighter budgets and seek independent, active experiences, are unlikely to see the region as relevant to them. Furthermore, budget accommodation is scarce, and public transport between villages is infrequent, making it difficult to explore without a car.

Firstly, the tourist board should partner with local landowners to develop affordable accommodation such as hostels and campsites. Secondly, a regional travel pass offering unlimited bus and boat travel for a fixed price would make independent exploration far easier. Thirdly, the region's outstanding opportunities for kayaking, hiking and cycling should be promoted through social media campaigns featuring young travel content creators, whose recommendations carry considerable weight with this audience. Finally, an annual outdoor music and adventure festival could raise the region's profile internationally.

Benefits
Attracting young visitors would help diversify the local economy. Unlike older tourists, who tend to visit in summer, young travellers often travel outside peak season, helping to sustain businesses throughout the year. Moreover, those who enjoy the region when young often return later in life with families of their own.

Proposal for an Employee Health Programme

Introduction
This proposal recommends a set of initiatives designed to improve the physical and mental health of employees. It is informed by sickness absence records and a recent staff survey.

Current issues
Absence due to back problems and stress-related illness has risen steadily over the past three years. Most employees spend the majority of the day seated at their desks, frequently eating lunch in front of their screens. In the survey, nearly half reported feeling exhausted at the end of the working week, and many said they found it difficult to fit exercise into their schedules.

Suggested initiatives
I propose, first of all, that the company offer ergonomic assessments of workstations and provide adjustable desks for those who would benefit. Secondly, staff could be encouraged to take proper lunch breaks away from their desks, perhaps by creating a more attractive break area. Thirdly, the company could arrange discounted membership at a nearby gym and organise lunchtime walking groups and yoga sessions on site. Finally, a confidential counselling service should be made available to employees experiencing stress or personal difficulties.

Benefits for the company
Although these initiatives involve some initial expense, they are likely to prove cost-effective. Healthier employees take fewer sick days, and research suggests that workplace wellbeing programmes improve concentration and productivity. Rethinking Progress: A Review of 'The Long View'

It is rare for a book to genuinely alter the way one sees the world, but 'The Long View' did precisely that for me. Its central argument is deceptively simple: by almost every measurable standard, from life expectancy to literacy and child mortality, human wellbeing has improved dramatically over the past two centuries, yet most of us believe things are getting worse.

The author, a statistician, builds her case meticulously, drawing on a wealth of data presented in clear, often strikingly designed charts. What elevates the book above a mere catalogue of statistics, however, is her exploration of why our perceptions are so distorted. She examines how news media, by focusing on sudden disasters rather than gradual improvements, and our own psychological bias towards negative information combine to create a persistently gloomy outlook.

Reading it challenged my habit of assuming the worst. I had, for instance, grossly underestimated how many children worldwide now attend school. Yet the book is far from complacent. The author is careful to stress that progress is neither inevitable nor evenly shared, and that acknowledging past achievements should encourage, rather than discourage, efforts to tackle remaining problems.

If the book has a flaw, it is that the later chapters become somewhat repetitive, and readers already familiar with the data may find little that is new.

Nevertheless, I would wholeheartedly recommend it, particularly to anyone who feels overwhelmed by negative news. It offers not naive optimism, but something more valuable: a sense of perspective grounded in evidence.

Dining in the Dark: An Evening at Blind Taste

The concept behind Blind Taste is as simple as it is unsettling: diners eat their entire meal in complete darkness, guided and served by waiters who are themselves visually impaired. Having been sceptical about what I assumed would be little more than a gimmick, I left with a genuine appreciation of how profoundly sight shapes our experience of food.

On arrival, guests choose from a set menu without being told exactly what it contains, before being led in a line, hand on shoulder, into the pitch-black dining room. The initial disorientation is considerable; simply locating one's glass becomes an achievement. Yet within minutes, the other senses seem to sharpen remarkably. Conversations become more animated, and flavours, textures and aromas take on an unexpected intensity.

The food itself was, for the most part, excellent. A starter of what turned out to be beetroot and goat's cheese was delicately balanced, and the slow-cooked lamb that followed was exceptionally tender. Dessert, a passion fruit mousse, proved somewhat overly sweet. Most impressive of all, though, was the service. Our waiter, Tom, navigated the room with effortless confidence and a wonderful sense of humour, putting nervous diners at ease.

At seventy pounds per person, Blind Taste is certainly not cheap, and those who simply want a satisfying meal could eat equally well elsewhere for less. However, as an experience that challenges perceptions, both of food and of disability, it is genuinely memorable. I would recommend it for a special occasion, ideally with companions who enjoy conversation.

Rising Waters: Art at the Edge of Climate Change

The City Gallery's latest exhibition brings together twenty artists from coastal communities around the world, each responding to the threat of rising sea levels. It is an ambitious undertaking, and while not every work succeeds, the exhibition as a whole leaves a lasting impression.

The opening room sets the tone powerfully. A vast installation of thousands of suspended glass droplets, gradually descending towards the floor, evokes both the beauty and the menace of water. Nearby, a series of photographs documents a fishing village in the Pacific before and after it was abandoned, the empty homes slowly reclaimed by the sea. These works communicate the human cost of climate change far more effectively than any statistics.

The exhibition's greatest strength lies in its emphasis on personal stories. Short video interviews with residents, played alongside many of the artworks, prevent the subject from becoming abstract. Particularly moving was the testimony of an elderly woman describing the graveyard where her parents are buried, now submerged at high tide.

That said, the exhibition is not without weaknesses. The later rooms feel overcrowded, and several pieces rely heavily on lengthy explanatory texts, suggesting the artwork alone does not convey its meaning. I also found myself wishing the curators had included more about how communities are adapting, which would have balanced the prevailing sense of loss with some cause for hope.

These reservations aside, 'Rising Waters' is a thought-provoking and often deeply affecting exhibition. It deserves to be seen by anyone who believes art can deepen our understanding of urgent global issues.

A Year with an E-Reader: Worth the Switch?

When I bought an e-reader last year, I fully expected it to end up abandoned in a drawer, as so many gadgets do. Twelve months on, it has become one of the few devices I use every single day, although my enthusiasm is not entirely unqualified.

The device's most obvious advantage is convenience. Being able to carry hundreds of books in a lightweight device has transformed travelling, and the ability to download a new title instantly is dangerously appealing. The screen, which mimics the appearance of paper, causes far less eye strain than a tablet, and the battery lasts for several weeks on a single charge. Features I initially dismissed as unnecessary, such as the built-in dictionary and adjustable font size, have proved surprisingly useful, particularly when reading in English.

However, certain drawbacks have become more apparent over time. I find it considerably harder to flick back through an e-book to find a particular passage, and the experience of reading illustrated books or maps is distinctly inferior. More significantly, e-books are often barely cheaper than paper copies, and they cannot be lent, resold or passed on in the same way. In effect, one is buying a licence rather than owning a book outright.

So, is it worth the investment? For frequent readers and travellers, undoubtedly. The device has encouraged me to read more than I have in years. Nevertheless, I have found myself returning to printed books for anything I truly treasure. The e-reader complements, rather than replaces, a traditional bookshelf.

Review: 'Data Analysis for Beginners' (Online, Twelve Weeks)

Having spent most of my career avoiding spreadsheets, I enrolled on this course with a degree of trepidation. Twelve weeks later, I can confidently say it has been one of the most worthwhile investments of time I have made, though it is not without its shortcomings.

The course is logically structured, beginning with basic statistical concepts before progressing to data visualisation and an introduction to programming. Each week combines short video lectures, practical exercises using real data sets and a live online seminar. This blend works well: the videos explain concepts clearly, while the exercises ensure that knowledge is consolidated through practice rather than passively absorbed.

The quality of teaching was, on the whole, impressive. The lead tutor has a gift for making complex ideas accessible, frequently using examples drawn from everyday life. Questions posted in the discussion forum were usually answered within a day. The materials, however, were less consistent. Several exercises contained errors, and the programming section felt rushed, leaving many participants struggling to keep up. It would benefit from being extended by at least two weeks.

The course would particularly suit professionals who need to interpret data in their work but have little mathematical background. It requires a substantial commitment of around eight hours a week, so those with demanding schedules should plan accordingly. Anyone with prior programming experience, by contrast, may find the early weeks rather slow.

Overall, despite some flaws, I would strongly recommend the course. It has given me not only practical skills but also the confidence to approach data without fear.

From Page to Screen: 'The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter'

Adapting a much-loved novel for the screen is a notoriously risky undertaking, and expectations for this film were extraordinarily high. The result is a visually stunning adaptation that captures much of the book's atmosphere, even if it inevitably sacrifices some of its depth.

The story follows Ellen, a young woman who returns to the remote island where she grew up after her father's death, only to uncover letters revealing a secret he kept for forty years. Alternating between the present and her father's youth, the narrative gradually pieces together a story of loyalty, loss and an impossible choice.

Visually, the film is superb. The windswept landscapes and the brooding lighthouse convey the isolation of island life more powerfully than words ever could, and the performances, particularly that of the actor playing the young father, are subtle and convincing. Where the film falls short, however, is in its treatment of Ellen's inner life. In the novel, her reflections, revealed through a first-person narrative, are the emotional heart of the story. On screen, they are reduced to occasional voice-overs, and her transformation consequently feels abrupt. Several secondary characters have also been removed entirely, which simplifies the plot but loses some of its richness.

Ultimately, I prefer the book. Its slow, introspective pace allows the reader to inhabit Ellen's thoughts in a way that the film, constrained by its two-hour running time, cannot replicate. Nonetheless, the adaptation stands as a beautiful work in its own right and may well encourage viewers to discover the novel for themselves.

items.sampleAnswer:
The Art of Slowing Down

When did you last do just one thing at a time? Not eat lunch while answering emails, or watch a film while scrolling through your phone, but give your undivided attention to a single activity? If you struggle to remember, you are far from alone.

Modern life seems to have accelerated to a dizzying pace. Technology, which promised to save us time, has instead filled every spare moment with notifications, messages and endless content. We are constantly reachable, perpetually busy and, paradoxically, often less productive than ever. Busyness has become a badge of honour; admitting that we have free time can almost feel like a confession of failure.

Yet there is growing evidence that slowing down brings genuine benefits. Concentrating on one task at a time tends to produce better work in less time, since switching between activities carries a hidden cost. Unhurried meals improve digestion, and time spent simply walking or daydreaming allows the mind to process experiences and generate creative ideas. Perhaps most importantly, slowing down enables us to notice and appreciate the small pleasures that make life meaningful.

So how can we reclaim a more measured pace? Start small. Leave your phone in another room during meals, or designate one evening a week as screen-free. Walk rather than drive for short journeys. Before agreeing to a new commitment, ask yourself whether it truly matters to you. And occasionally, allow yourself to do absolutely nothing at all.

Slowing down is not about doing less for its own sake. It is about choosing, deliberately, what deserves our time, and giving it the attention it deserves.

What I Wish I'd Known Before Starting My First Job

On my first day as a junior marketing assistant, I arrived convinced that success depended on one thing: proving how clever I was. I had excellent grades and a head full of theories, and I assumed my new colleagues would be suitably impressed. It took me the best part of a year to realise how mistaken I had been.

The first lesson was that asking questions is a strength, not a weakness. Terrified of appearing incompetent, I would spend hours struggling with tasks that a colleague could have explained in five minutes. When I eventually confessed my confusion to my manager, she was baffled that I hadn't simply asked. Experienced professionals, I discovered, generally respect curiosity far more than pretended knowledge.

The second lesson concerned relationships. At university, my results depended largely on my own efforts. At work, almost everything depends on cooperation. The receptionist, the IT technician and the colleague in accounts are not obstacles to be navigated but people whose goodwill can make your job immeasurably easier. Taking time to get to know them was one of the best investments I ever made.

Finally, I learned that it is perfectly acceptable not to have your entire career mapped out. I had imagined my first job as the first step on a fixed ladder; in fact, it was the beginning of a winding path that has taken me in directions I could never have predicted.

My advice, then, to anyone starting out? Listen more than you speak, value every colleague, and don't be afraid to admit what you don't know. Competence will follow.

The Map in Our Pocket

There was a time, not so long ago, when getting lost was an ordinary part of life. Travellers unfolded paper maps on car bonnets, asked strangers for directions and occasionally ended up somewhere entirely unexpected. Today, thanks to satellite navigation on our smartphones, such experiences have become almost unthinkable.

The benefits are undeniable. Navigation apps guide us through unfamiliar cities with astonishing accuracy, suggest faster routes to avoid traffic and estimate arrival times to the minute. For delivery drivers and emergency services, the technology has transformed efficiency; for nervous travellers, it has removed a major source of anxiety. It has even made exploration more accessible, encouraging people to venture into places they might once have avoided for fear of getting lost.

Yet this convenience may come at a subtle cost. Research suggests that people who rely heavily on navigation apps develop a weaker mental map of their surroundings, since they no longer need to pay attention to landmarks or remember routes. We follow the blue dot obediently, eyes fixed on the screen, often barely noticing the streets we pass through. Something is also lost in the decline of asking for directions, which once prompted countless small encounters with strangers.

On balance, few of us would willingly return to the days of paper maps, and I am certainly not among them. However, it may be worth occasionally switching off the app, looking around and trusting our own sense of direction. Getting a little lost, after all, can sometimes lead us exactly where we need to be.

Is Failure the Best Teacher?

We are often told that failure is the key to success. Inventors celebrate their thousands of unsuccessful prototypes, and entrepreneurs proudly recount the businesses that collapsed before their breakthrough. Yet for most students, failure feels less like a valuable lesson and more like a disaster to be avoided at all costs.

This fear is hardly surprising. From an early age, we are judged by grades and test scores, and mistakes are marked in red. In a competitive education system, a single poor result can seem to close doors permanently. It is no wonder that many students choose safe options rather than risk falling short.

And yet, failure can teach lessons that success rarely does. When something goes wrong, we are forced to analyse why, to question our assumptions and to try a different approach. I learned far more from the essay that received my lowest grade than from any of my best, because it made me confront weaknesses I had been ignoring. Failure also builds resilience: discovering that we can recover from setbacks makes us more willing to take on challenges in future.

However, the idea that failure is always beneficial can be misleading. Failure teaches only when it is followed by reflection and support. Repeated failure without guidance, by contrast, tends to erode confidence and motivation rather than building them.

So is failure the best teacher? Perhaps not on its own. But combined with honest reflection and encouragement, it can be one of the most powerful teachers we have. The real challenge for schools is to create environments in which it is safe to fail.

The Power of Repair

When the zip on my favourite jacket broke last winter, my first instinct was to throw it away and buy a new one. It was cheaper, quicker and, frankly, what everybody does. Instead, on a friend's recommendation, I took it to a local repair café. Twenty minutes and a few pounds later, it was as good as new. That small decision has changed the way I think about everything I own.

Repairing rather than replacing might seem trivial, but its potential impact is considerable. The manufacture of clothes, electronics and household goods accounts for a substantial share of global carbon emissions, and millions of tonnes of usable items end up in landfill every year. Extending the life of products by even a year or two significantly reduces the demand for new ones, along with the resources and energy required to produce them.

So why don't more of us repair things? Partly, it is a matter of skills: many people have simply never learned how. Products are also increasingly designed in ways that make repair difficult, with glued components and a lack of spare parts. And, perhaps most importantly, a culture of cheap, disposable goods has made replacing things feel normal.

Fortunately, attitudes are beginning to shift. Repair cafés, where volunteers help people fix their belongings for free, are spreading rapidly, and several governments have introduced 'right to repair' laws requiring manufacturers to supply spare parts. Each of us can contribute by learning basic repair skills and choosing durable products.

The next time something breaks, before reaching for your wallet, ask yourself: could this be fixed?

items.sampleAnswer:
Dear Editor,

I read with some frustration last week's article, 'The Lazy Generation', which claimed that today's young people lack the work ethic of their parents and grandparents. While I appreciate that the writer was expressing a personal opinion, I feel the article presented a deeply unfair picture.

Firstly, the evidence simply does not support such a sweeping claim. Many young people today combine full-time study with part-time jobs in order to cope with rising tuition fees and living costs. Others work in insecure, short-term contracts, often for several employers at once, with none of the job security previous generations enjoyed. Far from being lazy, they frequently work harder for less reward.

Secondly, young people are making significant contributions in areas the article overlooked entirely. In our own town, it was teenagers who organised the river clean-up last spring, and young volunteers run much of the weekend food bank.

What may have changed is not young people's willingness to work, but their attitude towards it. Many are unwilling to sacrifice their mental health for the sake of their careers and value flexibility and meaningful work. Rather than regarding this as laziness, we might view it as a reasonable response to lessons learned from older generations.

Generalisations about any age group are rarely accurate. I hope future articles will offer a more balanced perspective.

Yours faithfully,
Pham Thu Ha

items.prompt: A former colleague has applied for a management position and asked you to write a letter of reference. Write the letter to the hiring company.
items.promptVi: Một đồng nghiệp cũ ứng tuyển vị trí quản lý và nhờ bạn viết thư giới thiệu. Hãy viết thư gửi công ty tuyển dụng.
points: explain how you know the candidate
describe their skills and qualities with examples

items.sampleAnswer:
Dear Mr Hoffmann,

I am writing to recommend Ms Vo Thi Mai for the position of Operations Manager at your company. I was Ms Vo's line manager at Delta Logistics for four years, during which time she progressed from logistics coordinator to senior team leader.

Throughout this period, Ms Vo consistently demonstrated exceptional organisational and problem-solving abilities. When a major supplier unexpectedly went out of business in 2022, she devised and implemented an alternative supply plan within a week, ensuring that our clients experienced no delays. She also led a project to streamline our warehouse procedures, which reduced processing times by almost twenty per cent.

What distinguishes Ms Vo, however, is not only her technical competence but also her ability to motivate others. As a team leader, she created an environment in which colleagues felt comfortable raising concerns and suggesting improvements, and staff turnover in her team was the lowest in the department. She handles conflict calmly and fairly, and she is always willing to support less experienced colleagues.

Given her combination of strategic thinking, reliability and interpersonal skills, I am confident that Ms Vo would excel in a management role. She would be a tremendous asset to your organisation.

Please do not hesitate to contact me should you require any further information.

Yours sincerely,
Daniel Brooks
Regional Director, Delta Logistics

items.prompt: You organised an international conference that experienced several problems. Write an email to the participants apologising and explaining what will be done differently next year.
items.promptVi: Bạn tổ chức một hội nghị quốc tế gặp nhiều trục trặc. Hãy viết email xin lỗi người tham dự và giải thích những điều sẽ thay đổi năm tới.
items.sampleAnswer:
Dear Participants,

Thank you once again for attending this year's International Education Forum. While we were delighted by the quality of the presentations and discussions, we are well aware that several aspects of the event fell short of the standards you were entitled to expect, and I would like to apologise sincerely on behalf of the organising committee.

In particular, many of you experienced lengthy queues at registration on the first morning, and a number of sessions started late as a result. We also received numerous complaints about the poor Wi-Fi connection and the fact that two of the workshop rooms were too small for the number of attendees.

Having reviewed the event, we have identified the main causes. Registration numbers were almost forty per cent higher than anticipated, and our booking system did not alert us early enough to adjust our arrangements. In addition, the venue's network was not designed to support such a large number of devices.

For next year's forum, we will introduce online pre-registration with digital badges, which should eliminate queues almost entirely. We have also secured a larger venue with a dedicated high-speed network, and workshops will require advance booking so that room sizes can be matched to demand.

We greatly value your feedback and hope to welcome you again next year.

Kind regards,
Le Van Hoang
Conference Coordinator

items.prompt: A friend from another country is considering moving to your city to study and has asked for your honest advice. Write an email.
items.promptVi: Một người bạn nước ngoài đang cân nhắc chuyển đến thành phố bạn để học và nhờ bạn khuyên thật lòng. Hãy viết email.
points: the advantages of living in your city
items.sampleAnswer:
Hi Sofia,

It was lovely to hear from you, and I'm thrilled you're thinking of coming to Hanoi! You asked for an honest picture, so here it is – the good, the bad and the chaotic.

Let's start with the positives. The cost of living is considerably lower than in most European cities, so your scholarship would stretch much further than you might expect. The food is incredible and astonishingly cheap, and there's always something going on, from street festivals to live music. People are generally warm and welcoming towards foreigners, especially if you make an effort with a few words of Vietnamese.

That said, it isn't always easy. The traffic is genuinely overwhelming at first, and crossing the road requires a certain amount of courage. The summers are extremely hot and humid, and air pollution can be quite bad in winter. You might also find the language barrier frustrating outside the city centre, as English isn't widely spoken everywhere.

My advice would be to find accommodation within walking or cycling distance of the university, so you're not dependent on motorbikes from day one. Take a basic Vietnamese course before you arrive – even a little goes a long way. And join some university clubs early on; they're the quickest way to make friends.

If you do decide to come, you'll have a guaranteed tour guide in me! Let me know if you have any other questions.

Lots of love,
Linh

items.prompt: You are a member of a sports club whose facilities have deteriorated. Write an email to the club committee requesting improvements.
items.promptVi: Bạn là thành viên một câu lạc bộ thể thao có cơ sở vật chất xuống cấp. Hãy viết email gửi ban điều hành đề nghị cải thiện.
points: describe the problems with the facilities
suggest improvements and how they might be funded
items.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,

I am writing on behalf of a group of members to raise our concerns about the condition of the club's facilities, which has deteriorated noticeably over the past year.

The most pressing issue concerns the changing rooms. Several showers no longer work properly, the heating is unreliable, and a number of lockers have broken locks, which has led to at least two thefts. In addition, the surface of the second tennis court has become uneven and slippery after rain, and the floodlights frequently fail during evening sessions.

These problems are having a significant impact on members. Several people have told me they are reluctant to renew their membership, and attendance at evening training has fallen considerably. More seriously, the condition of the court poses a genuine risk of injury, which could also expose the club to liability.

We would therefore like to propose that repairs to the changing rooms and the court be treated as a priority. To help fund these improvements, the club could organise a fundraising tournament open to non-members, apply for a grant from the city's community sports fund, or introduce a modest, temporary increase in membership fees. Many members have indicated that they would be willing to pay slightly more if they could see a clear improvement in facilities.

We would be grateful if this matter could be discussed at the next committee meeting, and we would be happy to help in any way.

Kind regards,
Bui Quang Huy
